ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Discovery of DNA Structure
● In the 1950s Rosalind Franklin 
performed X-Ray Crystallography
of DNA
○ Her work revealed a pattern 
that was regular and repetitive
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Photographs of Rosalind Franklin and an X-ray diffraction image are connected visually to a double-helix model.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Discovery of DNA Structure
● During the same time, Edwin Chargaff analyzed 
DNA samples from different species
○ He found the following rule held true for all species:
■ The amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine
■ The amount of cytosine equals the amount of guanine
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Chemical structures of A–T and G–C base pairs show hydrogen-bonding positions.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Nucleotide Structure
● Purines
○ Double ring structure 
(A, G)
● Pyrimidines
○ Single ring structure 
(C, U, T)
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Chemical ring diagrams distinguish purines from pyrimidines.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Nucleotide Pairing
● The base pairs are held together by hydrogen 
bonds
● Adenine and thymine have two hydrogen bonds
● Cytosine and guanine have three hydrogen bonds
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Structural diagrams show two hydrogen bonds in A–T and three in G–C.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
1. Think ahead to DNA replication. How might 
hydrogen bonds aid in this process?
a. Answer: hydrogen bonds allow for the DNA 
strands to be easily separated during the 
replication process
2. A DNA sample is analyzed and you find that 22% 
is cytosine, how much thymine would you expect 
in the sample?
a. Answer: 28%

Discovery of DNA Structure
● Watson and Crick combined the findings of 
Franklin (helix shape) and Chargaff (base pairing) 
to create the first 3D, double helix model of DNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Historical photographs accompany a 3D double-helix model.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Key Features of DNA Structure
1. DNA is a double stranded helix 
2. DNA strands are antiparallel
a. One strand runs 5’ to 3’, other strand runs in 
opposite, upside-down direction 3’ to 5’
b. 5’ end: free phosphate group
c. 3’ end: free hydroxyl group
a. Backbone: sugar-
phosphate
b. Center: 
nucleotides pairing
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: DNA diagram labels antiparallel 5′/3′ strands, sugar-phosphate backbone, and paired bases in the center.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Key Function of DNA
● DNA is the primary source of heritable information
○ Genetic information is 
stored in and passed from 
one generation to the next 
through DNA
■ Exception: RNA is the 
primary source of 
heritable information in 
some viruses
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Chromosome-to-DNA packing diagram includes nucleosomes/histones, centromere, telomeres, and the double helix.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic DNA
● DNA found in nucleus
● Linear chromosomes
● DNA is in nucleoid region
● Chromosomes are circular
Eukaryotic Cells Prokaryotic Cells
● Prokaryotes (and some eukaryotes) also contain 
plasmids
○ Small, circular DNA molecules that are separate 
from the chromosomes
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Side-by-side prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell/chromosome diagrams contrast nucleoid/circular DNA with nucleus/linear DNA.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Plasmids
● Plasmids replicate independently from the 
chromosomal DNA
○ Primarily found in prokaryotes
■ Contain genes that may be useful to the 
prokaryote when it is in a particular 
environment, but may not be required for 
survival 
PlasmidsChromosomal DNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Bacterial cell diagram distinguishes chromosomal DNA from separate plasmids.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Plasmids
● Plasmids can be manipulated in laboratories
○ Plasmids can be removed from bacteria, then a 
gene of interest can be inserted into the plasmid to 
form recombinant plasmid DNA
○ When the recombinant plasmid is inserted back 
into the bacteria the gene will be expressed
PlasmidsChromosomal DNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Bacterial cell diagram supports recombinant-plasmid manipulation and reintroduction.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Plasmids
● Bacteria can exchange genes found on plasmids 
with neighboring bacteria 
○ Once DNA is exchanged the bacteria can 
express the genes acquired
○ Helps with survival of prokaryotes
PlasmidsChromosomal DNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Bacterial cell diagram supports plasmid-mediated gene exchange.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text: RNA vs DNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Side-by-side RNA and DNA molecular diagrams show single- versus double-stranded architecture and U versus T.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
RNA vs DNA
● Deoxyribonucleic acid
● Double stranded
● A=T and C=G
DNARNA
● Ribonucleic acid
● Single stranded
● A=U and C=G

Quick Review
1. What was Chargaff’s rule?
a. Answer: in any species, the amount of A=T 
and amount of C=G in the DNA
2. What comprises the backbone of DNA?
a. Answer: sugar-phosphate groups
3. Which nucleotides are purines?
a. Answer: adenine and guanine
4. What type of bond holds together nucleotides?
a. Answer: hydrogen bonds

Quick Review
5. Summarize the scientific contributions of 
Chargaff, Franklin, and Watson and Crick
a. Chargaff: A=T, C=G
b. Franklin: helix shape of DNA
c. Watson and Crick: full 3D model of DNA
6. What are some key differences between RNA 
and DNA?
a. Answer: DNA is double stranded and adenine  
bonds to thymine. RNA is single stranded and 
adenine bonds to uracil

Practice FRQ
Many species of bacteria are becoming resistant to antibiotics. 
Recently, studies have analyzed the chromosomal DNA of antibiotic 
resistant bacteria. One bacteria studied is methicillin-resistant 
Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Researchers have found that its 
chromosomal DNA does not contain the genes for antibiotic 
resistance. They also found that when MRSA is cultured with a non-
resistant bacteria, the non-resistant bacteria becomes antibiotic 
resistant a) Identify the location of the antibiotic resistant genes. b) 
Discuss how the antibiotic resistant genes are being transmitted to 
non-resistant bacteria when cultured together.
a) The genes are likely located on plasmids
b) The genes for antibiotic resistance are being transmitted through 
the plasmids. MRSA can exchange genes found on plasmids with 
neighboring bacteria. The genes are then expressed.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
DNA Replication
● DNA replicates during the S phase of the cell cycle
● How does DNA replicate?

Models of DNA Replication
● There were 3 alternative models for DNA 
replication
Conservative Semi Conservative Dispersive
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Three schematic models compare conservative, semiconservative, and dispersive replication.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Models of DNA Replication
● Conservative model
○ The parental strands direct 
synthesis of an entirely new 
double stranded molecule
■ The parental strands are fully 
“conserved”
Conservative
Parental 
strands
Parental 
strands
New 
strands
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Conservative replication diagram preserves parental duplex and produces a wholly new duplex.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Models of DNA Replication
● Semi conservative model
○ The two parental strands each 
make a copy of itself
■ After one round of replication 
the two daughter molecules 
each have one parental and 
one new strand
Semi Conservative
Parental 
strands
1 parental
1 new strand
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Semiconservative diagram shows one parental and one newly synthesized strand in each daughter DNA molecule.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Models of DNA Replication
● Dispersive model
○ The material in the two parental 
strands is dispersed randomly 
between the two daughter 
molecules
■ After one round of replication 
the daughter molecules contain 
a random mix of parental and 
new DNA
Dispersive
Parental 
strands
Mix of 
parental 
and new
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Dispersive diagram shows old and new DNA interspersed within daughter strands.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Which Model Is Correct?
In 1954 Meselson and Stahl performed an experiment 
using bacteria
Process:
1. Bacteria was cultured 
with a heavy isotope, 
15N
2. Bacteria was 
transferred to a 
medium with 14N, a 
light isotope
3. DNA was centrifuged 
and analyzed after 
each replication
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Meselson–Stahl workflow diagram shows 15N culture, transfer to 14N, centrifugation, and analysis across generations.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Semi-Conservative Model
By analyzing samples of DNA after each generation, 
it was found that the parental strands were following 
the semi-conservative model.
Semi-Conservative Model
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Density-gradient visual shows the expected band patterns supporting semiconservative replication after successive generations.

Steps in DNA Replication
1. DNA replication begins at sites called origins of 
replication
● Various proteins attach to the origin of replication 
and open the DNA to form a replication fork

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Steps in DNA Replication
2. Helicase will unwind the DNA strands at each 
replication fork
● To keep the DNA from re-bonding with itself, proteins 
called single strand binding proteins (SSBPs) bind 
to the DNA to keep it open
● Topoisomerase will help prevent strain ahead of the 
replication fork by relaxing supercoiling

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Steps in DNA Replication
3. The enzyme primase initiates replication by adding 
short segments of RNA, called primers, to the parental 
DNA strand
● The enzymes that synthesize DNA can only attach new 
DNA nucleotides to an existing strand of nucleotides
● Primers serve as the foundation for DNA synthesis

Steps in DNA Replication

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Steps in DNA Replication
4. Antiparallel elongation
● DNA Polymerase III (DNAP III) attaches to each 
primer on the parental strand and moves in the 3’ 
to 5’ direction
○ As it moves, it adds nucleotides to the new strand in 
the 5’ to 3’ direction
○ The DNAP III that follows helicase is known as the 
leading strand and it only requires one primer
○ The DNAP III on the other parental strand that moves 
away from helicase is known as the lagging strand
and requires many primers

5. The leading strand is synthesized in one continuous 
segment, but since the lagging strand moves away
from the replication fork it is synthesized in chunks
● Okazaki fragments: segments of the lagging strand

Putting it all Together

Problems at the 5’ End
● Since DNAP III can only add nucleotides to a 3’ 
end, there is no way to finish replication on the 5’ 
end of a lagging strand
○ Over many replications, this would mean that the 
DNA would become shorter and shorter
○ How are the genes on DNA protected from this?
■ Telomeres: repeating units of short nucleotide 
sequences that do not code for genes
● Form a cap at the end of DNA to help 
postpone erosion
● The enzyme telomerase adds telomeres to 
DNA

Proofreading and Repair
● As DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the new 
DNA strand, it proofreads the bases added
○ If errors still occur, mismatch repair will take 
place
■ Enzymes remove and replace the incorrectly 
paired nucleotide
■ If segments of DNA are damaged, nuclease can 
remove segments of nucleotides and DNA 
polymerase and ligase can replace the 
segments

Quick Review
1. If a parental DNA strand read: 5’- ACGTAC- 3’ 
what would a newly synthesized complementary 
strand read? 
a. Answer: 3’- TGCATG- 5’
2. Summarize the role of helicase, topoisomerase, 
and DNA Polymerase III.
a. Answer: helicase unzips the DNA, 
topoisomerase helps reduce strain, DNAP III 
adds nucleotides to the new strand of DNA

Quick Review
3. What direction does DNAP III move along the 
parental strand?
a. Answer: It moves 3’ to 5’ 
4. Why do Okazaki fragments occur on the lagging 
strand.
a. Answer: fragments occur because DNAP III 
moves away from the replication fork, so it has 
to replicate in chunks

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Proteins
● Proteins are polypeptides made up of amino acids
○ Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds
● Gene expression: the process by which DNA 
directs the synthesis of proteins
○ Includes two stages: transcription and translation
■ Occur in all organisms
DNA RNA Protein
Transcription Translation

Transcription and Translation
● Transcription: the synthesis of 
RNA using information from DNA
○ Allows for the “message” of 
the DNA to be transcribed
○ Occurs in the nucleus
● Translation: the synthesis of a 
polypeptide using information 
from RNA
○ Occurs at the ribosome
○ A nucleotide sequence 
becomes an amino acid
sequence

Types of RNA
As we go through transcription and translation there 
will be three key RNA molecules
1. Messenger RNA (mRNA)
2. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
3. Transfer RNA (tRNA)

Messenger RNA
● Messenger RNA is synthesized during 
transcription using a DNA template 
○ mRNA carries information from the DNA (at the 
nucleus) to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm

Transfer RNA
● Transfer RNA molecules are 
important in the process of 
translation
○ Each tRNA can carry a 
specific amino acid
○ Can attach to mRNA via their 
anticodon
■ A complementary codon 
to mRNA
○ Allow information to be 
translated into a peptide 
sequence

Ribosomal RNA
● rRNA helps form ribosomes
● Helps link amino acids together

The Genetic Code
● DNA contains the sequence of nucleotides that 
codes for proteins
○ The sequence is read in groups of three called 
the triplet code
● During transcription, only one DNA strand is 
being transcribed
○ Known as the template strand (also known as 
the noncoding strand, minus strand, or 
antisense strand)

The Genetic Code
● mRNA molecules formed 
are antiparallel and 
complementary to the 
DNA nucleotides
○ Base pairing: A=U and 
C=G
○ The mRNA nucleotide 
triplets are called 
codons
■ Codons code for 
amino acids

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
The Genetic Code
● 64 different codon 
combinations
○ 61 code for amino 
acids
○ 3 are stop codons
○ Universal to all life
● Redundancy: more 
than one codon code 
for each amino acid
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Codon chart visual accompanies the counts of codons and redundancy.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
The Genetic Code
Example: the fat cat ate the rat
● If the reading frame shifts even 
by one letter, it will produce a 
completely different outcome
○ Hef atc ata tet her at
Reading frame: the codons on the mRNA must be 
read in the correct groupings during translation to 
synthesize the correct proteins
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Reading-frame word analogy visually shows how a one-character shift changes grouping.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Check
1. If the DNA template strand reads: 3’-ACGAGA- 5’ 
what will the mRNA transcript read?
a. Answer: 5’- UGCUCU-3’
2. Using the mRNA transcript from #1, what amino 
acids will be produced during translation? (refer to 
a codon chart)
a. Answer: cysteine (cys) and serine (ser)
Steps of Transcription
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Section transition slide titled Steps of Transcription.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Transcription
There are three steps in transcription
1. Initiation
2. Elongation
3. Termination

Step 1: Initiation
● Transcription begins when RNA polymerase molecules 
attach to a promoter region of DNA 
○ Do not need a primer to attach 
○ Promoter regions are upstream of the desired gene 
to transcribe

Step 1: Initiation
● Eukaryotes:
○ Promoter region is called 
TATA box
○ Transcription factors help 
RNA polymerase bind
● Prokaryotes:
○ RNA polymerase can 
bind directly to promoter
Notice that the promoter is always upstream of the gene of 
interest to be transcribed
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Promoter/TATA-box diagram contrasts simplified eukaryotic and prokaryotic initiation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Step 2: Elongation
● RNA polymerase opens the DNA and reads the 
triplet code of the template strand
○ Moves in the 3’ to 5’ direction
■ The mRNA transcript elongates 5’ to 3’
Moves 3’ to 5’
Elongates 5’ to 3’
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Directional diagram labels RNA polymerase reading 3′→5′ while RNA elongates 5′→3′.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Step 2: Elongation
● RNA polymerase moves downstream
○ Only opens small sections of DNA at a time
■ Pairs complementary RNA nucleotides
■ The growing mRNA strand peels away from the 
DNA template strand
● DNA double helix then reforms
● A single gene can be transcribed simultaneously 
by several RNA polymerase molecules
○ Helps increase the amount of mRNA 
synthesized
■ Increases protein production
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Multiple RNA polymerases on one gene illustrate simultaneous transcription.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Step 3: Termination
Prokaryotes
● Transcription proceeds through a termination 
sequence
○ Causes a termination signal
■ RNA polymerase detaches
■ mRNA transcript is released and proceeds to 
translation
● mRNA does NOT need modifications

Step 3: Termination
Eukaryotes
● RNA polymerase transcribes a sequence of DNA 
called the polyadenylation signal sequence
○ Codes for a polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA)
■ Releases the pre-mRNA from the DNA
● Must undergo modifications before 
translation

Pre-mRNA modifications
There are three modifications that must occur to 
eukaryotic pre-mRNA before it is ready for translation
1. 5’ cap
2. Poly-A tail
3. RNA splicing
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Three-part pre-mRNA processing overview lists 5′ cap, poly-A tail, and RNA splicing.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Pre-mRNA modifications
1. 5’ cap (GTP): the 5’ end of the pre-mRNA receives a 
modified guanine nucleotide “cap”
2. Poly-A tail: the 3’ end of the pre-mRNA receives 50-
250 adenine nucleotides
● Both the 5’ cap and the poly-A tail function to:
○ Help the mature mRNA leave the nucleus
○ Help protect the mRNA from degradation
○ Help ribosomes attach to the 5’ end of the mRNA 
when it reaches the cytoplasm

Pre-mRNA modifications
3. RNA Splicing: sections of the pre-mRNA, called 
introns, are removed and then exons are joined together
a. Introns: intervening sequence, do not code for amino 
acids
b. Exons: expressed sections, code for amino acids
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Pre-mRNA diagram distinguishes introns and exons and shows splicing.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Pre-mRNA modifications
Why does splicing occur?
● A single gene can code for more than one kind of 
polypeptide
○ Known as alternative splicing
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Alternative-splicing diagram shows one pre-mRNA yielding different mature mRNA combinations.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Pre-mRNA modifications
Once all modifications have occurred, the pre-mRNA 
is now considered mature mRNA and can leave the 
nucleus and proceed to the cytoplasm for translation 
at the ribosomes

Quick Check
1. Discuss the overall “big picture” of transcription.
a. Answer: transcription writes down the 
information from the DNA and allows it to leave 
the nucleus to be translated into a protein
2. How does initiation differ between eukaryotes and 
prokaryotes?
a. Answer: eukaryotes require transcription factors 
to help RNA polymerase bind to the DNA, 
whereas prokaryotic RNA polymerase can bind 
directly to the DNA

ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Section transition graphic for Translation with a folded-protein image.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Translation
● Translation: the synthesis of a 
polypeptide using information from 
the mRNA
○ Occurs at the ribosome
○ A nucleotide sequence becomes 
an amino acid sequence
● tRNA is a key player in translating 
mRNA to an amino acid 
sequence

Transfer RNA
● tRNA has an anticodon region 
which is complementary and 
antiparallel to mRNA
● tRNA carries the amino acid that 
the mRNA codon codes for
○ ACU codes for Thr
● The enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA 
synthetase is responsible for 
attaching amino acids to tRNA
○ When tRNA carries an amino 
acid it is “charged” 5’ 3’
3’ 5’
mRNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: tRNA/mRNA diagram shows antiparallel codon–anticodon pairing and amino-acid attachment.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Ribosomes
● Translation occurs at the ribosome
○ Ribosomes have two subunits: small and large
○ Prokaryotic and eukaryotic ribosomal subunits 
differ in size
■ Prokaryotes: small subunit (30s) large subunit 
(40s)
■ Eukaryotes: small subunit (40s) large subunit 
(60s)
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Ribosome diagram supports comparison of small and large subunits.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Ribosomes
● The large subunit has three sites: A, P, and E
○ A site: amino acid site
■ Holds the next tRNA carrying an amino acid
○ P site: polypeptide site
■ Holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide 
chain
○ E site: exit site
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Large-subunit diagram labels A, P, and E sites.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Check
1. How does the tRNA interact with the mRNA?
a. Answer: through its anticodon
2. What codes for the amino acid?
a. Answer: the mRNA codon
3. What are the three sites on the large ribosomal 
subunit?
a. Answer: A, P, and E

Translation
Translation occurs in three stages
1. Initiation
2. Elongation
3. Termination

Step 1: Initiation
● Translation begins when the small ribosomal subunit 
binds to the mRNA and a charged tRNA binds to the 
start codon, AUG, on the mRNA
○ The tRNA carries methionine
○ Next, the large subunit binds
Note: the first tRNA 
carrying Met will go 
to the P site, every 
other tRNA will go 
to the A site first
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Initiation diagram places initiator tRNA at AUG and depicts small/large ribosomal subunits.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Step 2: Elongation
● Elongation starts when the next tRNA comes into the A site 
● mRNA is moved through the ribosome and its codons are 
read
● Each mRNA codon codes for 
a specific amino acid
○ Codon charts are used to 
determine the amino acid
● Since all organisms use the 
same genetic code, it 
supports the idea of common 
ancestry
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Codon-chart visual supports translation of mRNA codons into amino acids.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Step 2: Elongation
Elongation occurs in steps:
1. Codon recognition: the 
appropriate anticodon of the 
next tRNA goes to the A-site
2. Peptide bond formation: 
peptide bonds are formed that 
transfer the polypeptide to the 
A site tRNA
3. Translocation: The tRNA in the 
A site moves to the P site, the 
tRNA in the P site goes to the 
E site. The A site is open for 
the next tRNA
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Elongation diagram shows codon recognition, peptide-bond formation, and translocation through A/P/E sites.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Step 3: Termination
Termination occurs when a stop codon in the mRNA 
reaches the A site of the ribosome
● Stop codons do not code for amino acids
● The stop codon signals for a release factor
○ Hydrolyzes the bond that holds the polypeptide 
to the P site
○ Polypeptide releases
○ All translational units disassemble
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Termination diagram shows a stop codon, release factor, polypeptide release, and ribosome disassembly.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
Before we move on to protein folding, take a minute 
to review primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary 
protein structures
● Primary: chain of amino acids
● Secondary: coils and folds due to hydrogen bonds 
forming
● Tertiary: side chain interaction
● Quaternary: 2+ polypeptide chains interacting

Protein Folding
● As translation takes place, the growing polypeptide 
chain begins to coil and fold
○ Genes determine the primary structure
■ Primary structure determines the final shape
○ Some polypeptides require chaperone proteins 
to fold correctly and some require modification 
before it can be functional in the cell
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Protein-folding diagram links primary sequence to higher-order folding and chaperone assistance.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Putting it all Together
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h3b9ArupXZg

Retroviruses
Retroviruses, like HIV, are an 
exception to the standard 
flow of genetic information
● Information flows from 
RNA to DNA
○ Uses an enzyme 
known as reverse 
transcriptase
■ Pairs viral RNA to 
DNA
■ DNA then becomes 
part of the RNA

Practice FRQ
1. All living organisms need a transfer of information 
to allow for genes to direct the synthesis of 
proteins. Explain how genes are transcribed and 
translated to produce a functional protein.
Transcription allows for DNA to be transcribe to mRNA via the 
work of RNA polymerase. mRNA must be modified before it 
can leave the nucleus to go to the ribosome for translation. 
Translation turns the RNA nucleotide sequence into an amino 
acid sequence. Describe each stage (initiation, elongation, 
termination).

Practice FRQ
2. Compare and contrast translation in prokaryotes 
and eukaryotes.
In prokaryotes, translation occurs with transcription. In 
eukaryotes translation occurs after the mRNA has been 
modified. Ribosomes are responsible for translation, but the 
sizes differ in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, 30s/40s vs 
40s/60s. Lastly, translation can occur in the mitochondria and 
chloroplast of eukaryotes.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Section transition graphic for Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization shows DNA, transcription, mRNA, and translation within a eukaryotic cell.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Gene Expression
● Prokaryotes and eukaryotes must be able to 
regulate which genes are expressed at any given 
time
○ Genes can be turned “on” or “off” based on 
environmental and internal cues
■ On/off refers to whether or not transcription will 
take place
○ Allows for cell specialization

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Bacterial Gene Expression
● Operons: a group of genes that can be turned on 
or off
○ Operons have three parts:
■ Promoter: where RNA polymerase can attach
■ Operator: the on/off switch
■ Genes: code for related enzymes in pathway
● Operons can be repressible or inducible
○ Repressible (on to off): transcription is 
usually on, but can be repressed (stopped)
○ Inducible (off to on): transcription is usually 
off, but can be induced (started)
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Operon diagram identifies promoter, operator, and related structural genes.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Bacterial Gene Expression
● Regulatory gene: produces a repressor protein 
that binds to the operator to block RNA 
polymerase from transcribing the gene
○ Always expressed, but at low levels
○ Binding of a repressor to an operator is 
reversible
Before going through examples, lets review allosteric 
enzymes

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Allosteric Regulation: Activator
● Allosteric activator: substrate binds to allosteric 
site and stabilizes the shape of the enzyme so 
that the active sites remain open

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Allosteric Regulation: Inhibitor
● Allosteric inhibitor: substrate binds to allosteric 
site and stabilizes the enzyme shape so that the 
active sites are closed (inactive form)

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Repressible Operons
● Example: the trp operon
○ The trp operon in bacteria controls the 
synthesis of tryptophan
○ Since it is repressible, transcription is active
■ It can be switched off by a trp repressor
● Allosteric enzyme that is only active when 
tryptophan binds to it
● When too much tryptophan builds up in bacteria, 
tryptophan is more likely to bind to the repressor 
turning it active, which will then temporarily shut 
off transcription for tryptophan

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text: Overview: trp Operon
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: trp operon diagram contrasts repressor-bound transcription-off state with transcription-on state.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Inducible Operon
● Example: the lac operon
○ The lac operon controls synthesis of lactase, an 
enzyme that digests lactose (milk sugar)
○ Since it is inducible, transcription is off
■ A lac repressor is bound to the operator 
(allosterically active)
○ The inducer for the lac repressor is allolactose
■ When present it will bind to the lac repressor  
and turn the lac repressor off (allosterically 
inactive)
● The genes can now be transcribed

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Overview: lac Operon
Lac repressor is active 
and bond to the operator
binds to lac repressor and it 
becomes inactive
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: lac operon diagram contrasts active repressor bound to operator with allolactose-inactivated repressor.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Check
1. Compare and contrast the bacterial lac operon 
and trp operon.
a. Answer: both regulate transcription of genes. 
The trp operon is repressible, while the lac 
operon is inducible.
2. What are the three parts of an operon?
a. Answer: Promoter: where RNA polymerase can 
attach. Operator: the on/off switch. Genes: code 
for related enzymes in pathway

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Gene Expression
● The phenotype of a cell or organism is 
determined by a combination of genes that are 
expressed and the levels that they are expressed
○ Differences between cell types is known as 
differential gene expression

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Gene Expression
● Eukaryotic gene 
expression is regulated 
at different stages
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Multi-stage regulation diagram spans chromatin, transcription, RNA processing/export, translation, mRNA degradation, and protein processing/degradation.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Gene Expression
Chromatin structure:
● If DNA is tightly wound it is less 
accessible for transcription
● How can it be modified?
○ Histone acetylation adds 
acetyl groups to histones, 
which loosens the DNA
○ DNA methylation adds 
methyl groups to DNA, 
which causes the chromatin 
to condense
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Chromatin diagrams illustrate more accessible versus condensed chromatin associated with histone acetylation and DNA methylation.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Gene Expression
Epigenetic inheritance:
● Chromatin modifications do not 
alter the nucleotide sequence 
of the DNA, but they can be 
heritable to future generations
○ Modifications can be 
reversed, unlike mutations
○ Explains why one identical 
twin may inherit a disease 
while the other does not

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Gene Expression
Transcription initiation:
● Once chromatin modifications 
allow the DNA to be more 
accessible, specific transcription 
factors bind to control 
elements
○ Sections of non coding DNA 
that serve as binding sites
○ Gene expression can be 
increased or decreased by 
binding of activators or 
repressors to control elements
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Transcription-control diagram shows transcription factors/control elements regulating initiation.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Gene Expression
RNA processing:
● Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA
Translation Initiation
● Translation can be activated or 
repressed by initiation factors
● MicroRNAs and small 
interfering RNAs can bind to 
mRNA and degrade it or block 
translation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Post-transcriptional regulation diagram shows alternative splicing and small-RNA-mediated mRNA regulation.

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Development
● During embryonic development, cell division and 
cell differentiation occurs
○ Cells become specialized in their structure and 
function
○ Morphogenesis: the physical process that gives 
an organism its shape

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Development
● How do cells differentiate during early 
development?
○ Cytoplasmic determinants: substances in the 
maternal egg that influence cells
○ Induction: cell to cell signals that can cause a 
change in gene expression
● Both cytoplasmic determinants and induction 
influence pattern formation
○ A “body plan” for the organism
■ Homeotic genes map out the body structures

ppt_raw_slides.section: Regulation of Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Eukaryotic Development
● As cells differentiate, apoptosis plays a critical 
role
○ Apoptosis: programmed cell death 
■ Allows structures to take their form
● Example: if apoptosis did not occur during 
the development of human hands and feet 
we would be born with webbed fingers and 
toes

ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Section transition graphic for Mutations and Biotechnology includes a gel image.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Mutations
● Mutations: changes in the genetic material of a 
cell, which can alter phenotypes
○ Primary source of genetic variation
○ Normal function and production of cellular 
products is essential
■ Any disruption can cause new phenotypes
○ Changes can be large scale or small scale
■ Large scale: chromosomal changes
■ Small scale: nucleotide substitutions, 
insertions, or deletions

Small Scale Mutations
● Point mutations: change a single nucleotide pair 
of a gene
○ Substitution: the replacement of one 
nucleotide and its partner with another pair of 
nucleotides
■ Silent: change still codes for the same amino 
acid (remember: redundancy in the genetic 
code)
■ Missense: change results in a different amino 
acid
■ Nonsense: change results in a stop codon
Point Mutations
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Point-mutation table compares no mutation, silent, nonsense, and missense examples at DNA, mRNA, and protein levels.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Small Scale Mutations
● Frameshift mutation: when the reading frame of 
the genetic information is altered
○ Disastrous effects to resulting proteins
■ Insertion: a nucleotide is inserted
■ Deletion: a nucleotide is removed

Large Scale Mutations
Mutations that affect chromosomes
● Nondisjunction: when chromosomes do not 
separate properly in meiosis
○ Results in the incorrect number of chromosomes
■ Example: Down Syndrome- trisomy 21
● Translocation: a segment of one chromosome 
moves to another
● Inversions: a segment is reversed
● Duplications: a segment is repeated
● Deletions: a segment is lost

Natural Selection
● Any time mutations occur, they are subject to 
natural selection
○ Genetic changes can sometimes enhance the 
survival and reproduction of an organism

Increasing Genetic Variation
● Prokaryotes can exchange genetic material 
through horizontal gene transfer
● If there is a mutation that is beneficial to the 
survival and reproduction of that prokaryote then it 
can also be transferred 
○ Transformation: uptaking of DNA from a nearby cell
○ Transduction: viral transmission of genetic material
○ Conjugation: cell to cell transfer of DNA
○ Transposition: movement of DNA segments within 
and between DNA molecules
Biotechnology
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Section transition slide titled Biotechnology.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Biotechnology
● Both DNA and RNA can be manipulated through 
genetic engineering

Gel Electrophoresis
Gel electrophoresis: a 
technique used to separate 
DNA fragments by size
● DNA is loaded into wells 
on one end of a gel and 
an electric current is 
applied
○ DNA fragments are 
negatively charged so 
they move towards the 
positive electrode
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Gel electrophoresis diagram shows wells, DNA migration toward positive electrode, and size separation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
PCR
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): a method used in 
molecular biology to make several copies of a specific 
DNA segment
● Segments of DNA are amplified
● Results can be analyzed using gel electrophoresis

DNA Sequencing
DNA sequencing: the process of determining the 
order of nucleotides in DNA

ced_current_atoms.label: DNA/RNA as hereditary information
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genetic information is stored in and passed to subsequent generations through DNA molecules and, in some cases, RNA molecules.

ced_current_atoms.label: Typical prokaryotic chromosome form
ced_current_atoms.statement: Prokaryotic organisms typically have circular chromosomes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Typical eukaryotic chromosome form
ced_current_atoms.statement: Eukaryotic organisms typically have multiple linear chromosomes composed of DNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: Eukaryotic chromosome condensation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Eukaryotic chromosomes are condensed using histones and associated proteins.

ced_current_atoms.label: Plasmids
ced_current_atoms.statement: Prokaryotes and eukaryotes can contain plasmids, extra-chromosomal circular DNA molecules.

ced_current_atoms.label: Purines
ced_current_atoms.statement: Adenine and guanine are purines with double-ring structures.

ced_current_atoms.label: Pyrimidines
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cytosine, thymine, and uracil are pyrimidines with single-ring structures.

ced_current_atoms.label: Conserved complementary base pairing
ced_current_atoms.statement: Purines pair with pyrimidines: adenine pairs with thymine in DNA or uracil in RNA, and guanine pairs with cytosine.

ced_current_atoms.label: Replication preserves hereditary continuity
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA replication copies genetic information so it can be transmitted between cell and organismal generations.

ced_current_atoms.label: DNA synthesis direction
ced_current_atoms.statement: New DNA is synthesized in the 5′→3′ direction.

ced_current_atoms.label: Semiconservative replication
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA replication is semiconservative: each parental strand serves as a template for a complementary new strand, so each daughter DNA duplex contains one parental strand and one new strand.

ced_current_atoms.label: Helicase
ced_current_atoms.statement: Helicase unwinds the DNA strands at replication forks.

ced_current_atoms.label: Topoisomerase
ced_current_atoms.statement: Topoisomerase relaxes supercoiling ahead of the replication fork.

ced_current_atoms.label: DNA polymerase requires RNA primers
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA polymerase requires an RNA primer with an available 3′ end to initiate new DNA synthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Leading and lagging strand synthesis
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA polymerase synthesizes the leading strand continuously and the lagging strand discontinuously because both new strands must be synthesized 5′→3′ on antiparallel templates.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ligase joins lagging-strand fragments
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments on the lagging strand into a continuous strand.

ced_current_atoms.label: Replication enzyme-name scope guard
ced_current_atoms.statement: For the AP Exam, names of replication steps and particular enzymes beyond DNA polymerase, ligase, RNA polymerase, helicase, and topoisomerase are outside required scope.

ced_current_atoms.label: RNA sequence and structure determine function
ced_current_atoms.statement: The sequence of RNA bases together with RNA molecular structure determines RNA function.

ced_current_atoms.label: mRNA function
ced_current_atoms.statement: Messenger RNA carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes for translation.

ced_current_atoms.label: tRNA amino-acid specificity
ced_current_atoms.statement: Distinct tRNA molecules bind specific amino acids.

ced_current_atoms.label: tRNA anticodon pairing
ced_current_atoms.statement: Each tRNA has an anticodon that base-pairs with a complementary mRNA codon.

ced_current_atoms.label: tRNA recruitment during translation
ced_current_atoms.statement: tRNA is recruited to the ribosome so the mRNA sequence can direct the primary amino-acid sequence.

ced_current_atoms.label: rRNA as ribosome component
ced_current_atoms.statement: Ribosomal RNA is a functional building block of ribosomes and participates in protein synthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Transcription uses one DNA template strand
ced_current_atoms.statement: RNA polymerase uses a single DNA template strand to direct complementary RNA synthesis; this process is transcription.

ced_current_atoms.label: Transcription directionality
ced_current_atoms.statement: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA 5′→3′ while reading the DNA template 3′→5′.

ced_current_atoms.label: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA processing
ced_current_atoms.statement: In eukaryotic cells, a primary RNA transcript is modified before it functions as mature mRNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: Poly-A tail stability
ced_current_atoms.statement: Addition of a poly-A tail increases mRNA stability.

ced_current_atoms.label: 5′ GTP cap recognition
ced_current_atoms.statement: Addition of a 5′ GTP cap supports ribosomal recognition and also contributes to mRNA protection and handling.

ced_current_atoms.label: Intron excision and exon splicing
ced_current_atoms.statement: RNA processing removes introns and splices retained exons to produce mature mRNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: Alternative splicing
ced_current_atoms.statement: Alternative splicing retains different combinations of exons, allowing one pre-mRNA to generate different mature mRNA versions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Translation location
ced_current_atoms.statement: Translation occurs on ribosomes in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and on ribosomes associated with the cytoplasmic surface of rough ER in eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Coupled transcription and translation in prokaryotes
ced_current_atoms.statement: In prokaryotes, translation can begin on an mRNA while that mRNA is still being transcribed.

ced_current_atoms.label: Translation stages
ced_current_atoms.statement: Translation proceeds through sequential initiation, elongation, and termination stages.

ced_current_atoms.label: Start codon AUG
ced_current_atoms.statement: Translation initiates at AUG, the start codon that specifies methionine, through interactions among mRNA, rRNA/ribosome, and an initiator tRNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: Codons
ced_current_atoms.statement: The mRNA nucleotide sequence is read in three-nucleotide units called codons.

ced_current_atoms.label: Codon specifies amino acid
ced_current_atoms.statement: A codon specifies an amino acid or a translation stop signal, and amino-acid identity can be determined using a genetic-code chart.

ced_current_atoms.label: Genetic-code redundancy
ced_current_atoms.statement: Many amino acids are encoded by more than one codon.

ced_current_atoms.label: Near universality of genetic code
ced_current_atoms.statement: Nearly all living organisms use the same genetic code, supporting common ancestry.

ced_current_atoms.label: tRNA delivers amino acid
ced_current_atoms.statement: tRNA brings the amino acid specified by the mRNA codon to the ribosome.

ced_current_atoms.label: Polypeptide elongation
ced_current_atoms.statement: During elongation, amino acids are transferred to the growing polypeptide chain as peptide bonds form.

ced_current_atoms.label: Translation continues to stop codon
ced_current_atoms.statement: The ribosome advances along the mRNA until a stop codon is reached.

ced_current_atoms.label: Translation termination releases product
ced_current_atoms.statement: Translation terminates with release of the newly synthesized polypeptide/protein product and disassembly of the translation complex.

ced_current_atoms.label: Translation factor-name scope guard
ced_current_atoms.statement: Details and names of enzymes and factors involved in translation steps are outside AP Exam scope.

ced_current_atoms.label: Genetic-code memorization scope guard
ced_current_atoms.statement: Memorization of the genetic code is outside AP Exam scope except for the start codon AUG; students should use a supplied code chart.

ced_current_atoms.label: Retroviral reverse transcription
ced_current_atoms.statement: In retroviruses, reverse transcriptase copies viral RNA into DNA; the DNA can integrate into the host genome and then be transcribed and translated to generate viral progeny.

ced_current_atoms.label: Regulatory DNA sequences and proteins
ced_current_atoms.statement: Regulatory DNA sequences interact with regulatory proteins to control transcription.

ced_current_atoms.label: Constitutive and inducible expression
ced_current_atoms.statement: Some genes are constitutively expressed while others are inducible in response to internal or environmental conditions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Reversible epigenetic regulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Reversible modifications of DNA or histones can alter gene expression without changing the DNA nucleotide sequence.

ced_current_atoms.label: Gene-expression profile determines phenotype
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cell and organism phenotypes depend on which genes are expressed and the levels at which they are expressed.

ced_current_atoms.label: Differentiation and tissue-specific proteins
ced_current_atoms.statement: Observable cell differentiation reflects expression of genes that produce cell- or tissue-specific products.

ced_current_atoms.label: Sequential developmental gene expression
ced_current_atoms.statement: Induction of transcription factors during development can produce sequential patterns of gene expression.

ced_current_atoms.label: Gene-product amount and function influence phenotype
ced_current_atoms.statement: The functions and amounts of gene products help determine phenotype.

ced_current_atoms.label: Coordinated prokaryotic operon regulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Prokaryotes can coordinately regulate groups of genes using inducible or repressible operons.

ced_current_atoms.label: Coordinated eukaryotic regulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Groups of eukaryotic genes can be coordinately regulated when they respond to the same transcription factors.

ced_current_atoms.label: Promoter/enhancer recruitment of transcription machinery
ced_current_atoms.statement: RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind promoter or enhancer DNA sequences to regulate initiation of transcription.

ced_current_atoms.label: Regulatory-sequence position
ced_current_atoms.statement: Promoter and enhancer regulatory sequences can influence transcription from positions upstream or downstream of the transcription start site.

ced_current_atoms.label: Negative transcriptional regulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Negative regulatory molecules can inhibit gene expression by binding DNA and preventing or reducing transcription.

ced_current_atoms.label: Differential gene expression and specialization
ced_current_atoms.statement: Gene regulation creates differential gene expression, changing cell products and functions and thereby contributing to cell specialization.

ced_current_atoms.label: Small RNA regulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Certain small RNA molecules regulate gene expression, for example by affecting mRNA stability or translation.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mutation effects depend on molecular consequence
ced_current_atoms.statement: A DNA-sequence mutation can change the type or amount of nucleic acid/protein product and phenotype; mutations can be beneficial, detrimental, or neutral depending on their molecular and environmental consequences.

ced_current_atoms.label: Point substitution
ced_current_atoms.statement: A point mutation can substitute one nucleotide for another nucleotide.

ced_current_atoms.label: Frameshift mutation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Insertion or deletion of nucleotide(s) can shift the reading frame when the change is not in a multiple of three within a coding sequence.

ced_current_atoms.label: Nonsense mutation
ced_current_atoms.statement: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.

ced_current_atoms.label: Silent mutation
ced_current_atoms.statement: A silent mutation changes a nucleotide sequence without changing the encoded amino-acid sequence.

ced_current_atoms.label: Specific-mutation effect scope guard
ced_current_atoms.statement: Specific named mutations and their detailed effects are beyond AP Exam scope unless provided in a question context.

ced_current_atoms.label: Sources of random DNA mutation
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA replication/repair errors and external factors such as radiation or reactive chemicals can cause random DNA mutations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Environmental context of mutation effect
ced_current_atoms.statement: Whether a mutation is beneficial, detrimental, or neutral can depend on the environmental context.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mutations generate genetic variation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mutations create new genetic variation that can be inherited when present in transmissible genetic material.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cell-division errors can alter phenotype
ced_current_atoms.statement: Errors in mitosis or meiosis can change chromosome number or structure and thereby alter phenotype.

ced_current_atoms.label: Nondisjunction and chromosome number
ced_current_atoms.statement: Nondisjunction can produce cells with abnormal chromosome numbers (aneuploidy).

ced_current_atoms.label: Chromosome-number changes can disrupt development
ced_current_atoms.statement: Changes in chromosome number can cause altered phenotypes and developmental disorders.

ced_current_atoms.label: Chromosome-structure alterations
ced_current_atoms.statement: Alterations in chromosome structure can change gene dosage, gene integrity, or regulation and can lead to genetic disorders.

ced_current_atoms.label: Specific chromosome-disorder scope guard
ced_current_atoms.statement: Specific disorders caused by chromosome-number changes are beyond AP Exam scope unless supplied in context.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mutation connects genotype, phenotype, and selection
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genotypic changes can alter phenotypes on which natural selection acts; variants that enhance survival and reproduction in a given environment can increase in frequency.

ced_current_atoms.label: Transformation as horizontal gene transfer
ced_current_atoms.statement: Transformation increases prokaryotic genetic variation through uptake of DNA from the environment.

ced_current_atoms.label: Transduction as horizontal gene transfer
ced_current_atoms.statement: Transduction increases prokaryotic genetic variation through virus-mediated transfer of genetic information.

ced_current_atoms.label: Conjugation as horizontal gene transfer
ced_current_atoms.statement: Conjugation increases prokaryotic genetic variation through cell-to-cell transfer of DNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: Transposition
ced_current_atoms.statement: Transposition moves DNA segments within or between DNA molecules and can increase genetic variation.

ced_current_atoms.label: Viral recombination
ced_current_atoms.statement: Related viruses can recombine genetic information when they infect the same host cell.

ced_current_atoms.label: Conserved reproductive sources of variation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Reproductive processes that increase genetic variation are evolutionarily conserved across diverse organisms.

ced_current_atoms.label: Genetic engineering manipulates/analyzes nucleic acids
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genetic engineering techniques can be used to analyze and manipulate DNA and RNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: Gel electrophoresis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by their movement through a gel under an electric field, with fragment size strongly affecting migration under standard DNA-gel conditions.

ced_current_atoms.label: PCR denaturation
ced_current_atoms.statement: PCR amplification cycles include denaturation to separate template DNA strands.

ced_current_atoms.label: PCR primer annealing
ced_current_atoms.statement: PCR amplification cycles include annealing primers to complementary target sequences.

ced_current_atoms.label: PCR extension
ced_current_atoms.statement: PCR amplification cycles include polymerase-mediated extension to synthesize new DNA strands.

ced_current_atoms.label: Bacterial transformation as biotechnology
ced_current_atoms.statement: Bacterial transformation introduces foreign DNA into bacterial cells and can be used to propagate or express engineered DNA.

ced_current_atoms.label: DNA sequencing
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA sequencing determines the order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule.

ced_current_atoms.label: DNA profiles/fingerprints support comparison
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genetic-analysis techniques can produce sequence data or fragment patterns that allow comparisons among DNA samples.

ced_current_atoms.label: Biotechnology-detail scope guard
ced_current_atoms.statement: Detailed procedural knowledge of gel electrophoresis, PCR, bacterial transformation, and DNA sequencing is beyond AP Exam scope beyond the required functional principles.

cross_unit_dependencies.content: Nucleotide structure, purines/pyrimidines, phosphodiester backbone, DNA/RNA differences, complementary base pairing, 5′/3′ directionality, protein primary structure and peptide bonds.
Nucleus/nuclear pores, nucleolus, ribosomes, rough ER, cytosol, prokaryotic nucleoid, and compartmental context for transcription/translation.
Allosteric regulation and protein/enzyme structure-function principles used to interpret repressors and regulatory proteins.
S phase, cell cycle, signaling-induced changes in gene expression, and downstream cellular responses.
Genes/alleles/chromosomes, nondisjunction, meiosis, genetic variation, and reproductive processes that generate variation.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck calls Franklin’s DNA work “X-Ray Crystallography” and reduces the structural evidence to a regular/repetitive pattern.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve the classroom wording in the raw ledger. Canonically describe Franklin’s X-ray diffraction work as providing critical evidence for DNA’s helical structure and dimensions; do not imply she merely supplied a picture used by others.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Watson and Crick are presented as simply combining Franklin’s helix finding and Chargaff’s base-pairing result to make the first 3D double-helix model.
review_flags.resolution: Retain the historical example as teacher enrichment, while avoiding an oversimplified discovery narrative. Their model-building incorporated multiple lines of evidence, including Franklin’s diffraction data and Chargaff’s composition rules.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: A quick-review item asks what bond “holds together nucleotides” and answers hydrogen bonds.
review_flags.resolution: Distinguish phosphodiester bonds within each nucleic-acid backbone from hydrogen bonds between complementary bases across paired strands/regions.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: RNA is presented categorically as single stranded and DNA as double stranded.
review_flags.resolution: Use “typically” for cellular RNA/DNA structure. RNA often folds into paired regions, and some viral genomes depart from the usual cellular patterns.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: DNA replication is said to occur during S phase without organismal qualification.
review_flags.resolution: Treat S phase as the eukaryotic cell-cycle context. Prokaryotic chromosome replication is not organized into a eukaryotic S phase.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Semiconservative replication is described as parental strands each “make a copy of itself.”
review_flags.resolution: Use template language: each parental strand directs synthesis of a complementary new strand.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck names SSBPs, primase, DNA polymerase I/III, and other replication-specific components.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve these as teacher enrichment. Current AP scope requires DNA polymerase, ligase, RNA polymerase, helicase, and topoisomerase by name; additional replication enzyme names are not required.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck requires the term Okazaki fragments.
review_flags.resolution: Keep the term as teacher enrichment. Current CED requires understanding discontinuous lagging-strand fragments and ligase joining them but does not require “Okazaki fragment” by name.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Telomeres and telomerase are taught as the solution to end-replication problems.
review_flags.resolution: Scientifically retain as teacher enrichment; they are not current Unit 6 AP-required content.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Proofreading, mismatch repair, nuclease action, and detailed repair pathways are taught.
review_flags.resolution: Retain as enrichment and as conceptual support for mutation/repair. Current Unit 6 requires that replication/repair errors can cause mutations, without requiring detailed repair pathway names.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Transcription is stated to occur in the nucleus as a general definition.
review_flags.resolution: Qualify by cell type: eukaryotic nuclear genes are transcribed in the nucleus; prokaryotes have no nucleus, so transcription occurs in the cytoplasmic/nucleoid region.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: An anticodon is described as “a complementary codon to mRNA.”
review_flags.resolution: An anticodon is a three-nucleotide tRNA sequence complementary and antiparallel to an mRNA codon; it is not itself called a codon.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: DNA is broadly described as a nucleotide sequence that codes for proteins.
review_flags.resolution: Genes can encode polypeptides or functional RNAs, and much DNA is noncoding/regulatory. Use protein-coding genes when describing codon-based translation.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The genetic code is called universal to all life.
review_flags.resolution: Use the current CED wording “nearly all living organisms use the same genetic code,” acknowledging rare exceptions while preserving common ancestry reasoning.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The eukaryotic promoter region is equated with the TATA box and promoter placement is described as always upstream.
review_flags.resolution: A TATA box is one promoter element present in some eukaryotic genes, not the universal name for eukaryotic promoters. Regulatory sequences can have more varied architecture; current CED explicitly allows promoter/enhancer sequences upstream or downstream of the transcription start site.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Detailed prokaryotic/eukaryotic transcription termination mechanisms and AAUAAA sequence are taught.
review_flags.resolution: Retain as teacher enrichment. Current AP scope centers on transcription directionality and eukaryotic RNA processing, not memorization of detailed termination sequences.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Introns are equated with sequences that do not code for amino acids and exons with sequences that do code for amino acids.
review_flags.resolution: Use removed intron / retained exon definitions. Exons can include untranslated regions, so retained exon does not universally mean amino-acid-coding sequence.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and release factor are explicitly named as required translation machinery.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve as teacher enrichment; current CED excludes memorization of translation enzymes/factors beyond the salient mechanistic features.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck gives prokaryotic ribosomal subunits as 30S and 40S.
review_flags.resolution: Correct to 30S small + 50S large = 70S prokaryotic ribosome. Eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes are 40S small + 60S large = 80S. These sizes remain teacher enrichment, not AP-required memorization.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: A, P, and E ribosomal sites and detailed translocation sequence are emphasized.
review_flags.resolution: Retain as teacher enrichment. Students need the causal translation sequence, but the named site choreography is not explicitly required by the current CED.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The retrovirus slide ends by saying copied DNA “then becomes part of the RNA.”
review_flags.resolution: Correct the canonical mechanism: reverse-transcribed viral DNA can integrate into the host DNA/genome and subsequently be transcribed and translated.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The regulatory gene/repressor description is generalized as always expressed at low levels.
review_flags.resolution: Treat this as a simplified lac/trp model feature rather than a universal rule for all regulatory genes or repressors.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Allosteric regulators are called substrates and the trp repressor is called an allosteric enzyme.
review_flags.resolution: Use “allosteric regulator/effector,” not necessarily substrate. The trp repressor is a regulatory protein; tryptophan acts as a corepressor that binds and activates the repressor.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The lac operon is said to control synthesis of “lactase.”
review_flags.resolution: Use the bacterial lac operon accurately: lacZ encodes β-galactosidase, while other lac structural genes encode lactose permease and transacetylase. Do not equate the operon with the human intestinal lactase enzyme.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Histone acetylation is presented as always loosening DNA and DNA methylation as always condensing chromatin.
review_flags.resolution: Keep the introductory association but avoid universal causation. These modifications often correlate with accessible/repressed chromatin in common contexts, while effects are locus- and context-dependent.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Epigenetic inheritance is used to explain why one identical twin may “inherit a disease” while the other does not.
review_flags.resolution: Do not use “inherit” for discordant disease occurrence within a twin pair. Epigenetic state can contribute to persistent gene-expression differences, alongside environmental and stochastic influences; transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is context-dependent.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Morphogenesis, cytoplasmic determinants, induction, homeotic genes, and apoptosis are taught as developmental mechanisms.
review_flags.resolution: Retain as teacher enrichment. The current Unit 6 CED requires gene regulation, transcription-factor induction, differential expression, and cell specialization, not memorization of these additional developmental mechanism names.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Mutation is called the primary source of genetic variation.
review_flags.resolution: Use mutation as the ultimate source of new alleles/novel sequence variation, while recombination, segregation, horizontal transfer, and other processes also generate or redistribute genetic variation.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Frameshift mutations are described as having “disastrous effects,” and any insertion/deletion is implied to cause a frameshift.
review_flags.resolution: A coding-region insertion/deletion shifts the reading frame when its length is not a multiple of three; consequences vary by position and sequence and are not universally catastrophic.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Down syndrome/trisomy 21 is a named example, while the current CED excludes specific chromosome-number disorders.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve the example as teacher enrichment only; do not make named disorders required retrieval targets.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The current CED text itself uses “triploidy (aneuploidy)” when describing chromosome-number changes.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve the raw CED wording in the source atom trace but use scientifically correct canonical terminology: aneuploidy is gain/loss of individual chromosomes; triploidy is whole-set polyploidy, not aneuploidy.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck states that any time mutations occur, they are subject to natural selection.
review_flags.resolution: Natural selection acts on heritable phenotypic variation affecting reproductive success; many somatic or phenotypically silent mutations are not directly exposed to organismal natural selection.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Gel electrophoresis is described simply as separating DNA fragments by size.
review_flags.resolution: For standard agarose DNA gels, DNA has similar charge-to-mass ratio so size is the dominant determinant of migration; preserve the CED’s broader “size and charge” wording while teaching the usual DNA-gel mechanism accurately.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The PPT gives only a broad PCR definition and omits the current CED-required denaturation, primer annealing, and extension cycle.
review_flags.resolution: Add explicit AP-required canonical records for the three functional PCR stages from the current CED, verified against Campbell.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The PPT discusses control elements but does not explicitly teach enhancer sequences or that regulatory sequences may be downstream of the transcription start site.
review_flags.resolution: Add the current CED-required promoter/enhancer and upstream/downstream relationship as an AP-required coverage repair.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The PPT teaches inducible/repressible operons but does not clearly identify constitutive expression as a general AP-required comparison.
review_flags.resolution: Add a canonical AP-required constitutive-versus-inducible expression record from the current CED.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The PPT covers four prokaryotic horizontal-transfer mechanisms but omits recombination between related viruses co-infecting the same host cell.
review_flags.resolution: Add the missing current CED viral-recombination record as an AP-required coverage repair.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The current CED links conserved reproductive processes to increased genetic variation, while this relationship was fully taught in Unit 5 rather than repeated in Unit 6 slides.
review_flags.resolution: Carry the requirement into Unit 6 as a cross-unit prerequisite/reapplication record instead of inventing duplicate mnemonic content.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The CED requires bacterial transformation as a biotechnology method and DNA-sample comparison/profile reasoning beyond the PPT’s minimal technique descriptions.
review_flags.resolution: Lock these AP requirements explicitly and map earlier plasmid/transformation context where available; keep detailed procedures outside required scope.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences and associated structures at chromosome ends that buffer loss of coding sequence and help maintain chromosome-end integrity.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Telomerase can extend telomeric DNA using an RNA-containing reverse-transcriptase mechanism in cells where it is active.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Many DNA polymerases proofread newly added nucleotides, reducing replication errors.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: DNA repair systems can recognize damaged or mismatched DNA, remove erroneous/damaged nucleotides, and use intact sequence information to restore DNA.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.16

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Proteins are polypeptide chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; amino-acid sequence contributes to higher-order structure and function.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Gene expression is the use of information in a gene to produce a functional RNA or polypeptide product; for protein-coding genes it includes transcription and translation.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Transcription is DNA-directed synthesis of RNA by RNA polymerase.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Translation is synthesis of a polypeptide using the nucleotide sequence of mRNA as information at a ribosome.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: For a transcribed gene, RNA polymerase reads one DNA template strand; “template” or “noncoding” strand is preferred over treating alternate historical aliases as separate concepts.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: A reading frame is the grouping of an mRNA nucleotide sequence into consecutive codons; shifting the frame changes downstream codon groupings.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: The teacher sequence organizes transcription into initiation, elongation, and termination as a useful process model.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: A promoter is a DNA region where transcription machinery assembles to initiate transcription of a gene.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17/18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: A TATA box is a promoter DNA element found in some eukaryotic genes and can participate in assembly of transcription machinery; it is not present in every eukaryotic promoter.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_label: Multiple RNA polymerases increase transcript output
canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Multiple RNA polymerase molecules can transcribe the same gene at the same time, increasing RNA output from an active gene.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Many bacterial mRNAs can be translated without the eukaryotic cap/poly-A/splicing processing sequence and can be translated while transcription continues.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: In eukaryotic pre-mRNA processing, a transcribed polyadenylation signal helps specify cleavage and subsequent poly-A-tail addition; AAUAAA is a common signal sequence in the RNA.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_label: Functions of cap and poly-A tail
canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: The 5′ cap and poly-A tail contribute to mRNA stability, export/handling, and efficient translation initiation in eukaryotic cells.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: After appropriate processing, eukaryotic mature mRNA can be exported from the nucleus and used for translation in the cytoplasm.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the correct amino acids to their corresponding tRNAs, producing charged tRNAs; the enzyme name is teacher enrichment outside required AP memorization.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S (30S + 50S) and eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes are 80S (40S + 60S); these Svedberg values are enrichment and are not additive mass units.

canonical_catalog.canonical_label: Ribosomal A, P, and E sites

canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: During elongation, codon–anticodon recognition positions the incoming tRNA, peptide-bond formation transfers the growing chain, and translocation advances the ribosome/tRNAs along the mRNA.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Stop codons do not encode amino acids; termination machinery promotes release of the completed polypeptide and ribosomal complex disassembly.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: A nascent polypeptide begins folding during and after synthesis, and some proteins require chaperones or additional processing/modification to reach functional form.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.5/17

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: An operon is a cluster of functionally related bacterial genes regulated together from shared control DNA, allowing coordinated transcription.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: In the simplified bacterial operon model, the promoter recruits RNA polymerase, the operator is a regulatory DNA site, and adjacent structural genes encode related products.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: A repressor is a regulatory protein whose binding to regulatory DNA can decrease transcription; its binding may be reversible and controlled by small molecules.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Binding of a regulatory molecule at an allosteric site can change protein conformation and activity; the ligand need not be a substrate.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Unit 3 prerequisite; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.8/18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: In the E. coli trp operon, high tryptophan favors activation of the trp repressor through corepressor binding, reducing transcription of tryptophan-biosynthesis genes.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Tryptophan functions as a corepressor by binding the trp repressor protein and enabling it to bind operator DNA.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: In the E. coli lac operon, lactose availability can inactivate the lac repressor through allolactose, permitting transcription of genes involved in lactose uptake/metabolism.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Allolactose binds the lac repressor and reduces its operator-binding activity, acting as an inducer of lac-operon transcription.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: The lac operon includes genes such as lacZ encoding β-galactosidase and lacY encoding lactose permease; it should not be reduced to production of a single “lactase” enzyme.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Eukaryotic gene expression can be regulated at chromatin/transcriptional, RNA-processing/stability, translational, and post-translational stages.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Histone acetylation is commonly associated with more accessible chromatin and increased transcriptional potential at affected loci.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: DNA methylation can contribute to stable or reversible repression of gene expression in many eukaryotic contexts, depending on genomic location and regulatory system.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Some chromatin states and DNA/histone modifications can persist through cell division without altering nucleotide sequence; transgenerational persistence depends on biological context.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Noncoding regulatory DNA elements can bind transcription factors that increase or decrease transcription of target genes.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Alternative splicing can regulate which mature mRNA and protein isoforms are produced from a gene.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Campbell Biology 13e Ch.17/18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: microRNAs and small interfering RNAs can base-pair with target RNAs and promote RNA degradation or inhibit translation; the named subclasses are teacher enrichment beyond the CED’s broader small-RNA requirement.
canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.18

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Cell differentiation is the process by which cells develop specialized structures and functions through regulated gene expression.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Developmental gene-regulatory networks establish body pattern; homeotic genes are one class of developmental regulators that specify regional identity in many animals.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Apoptosis is regulated programmed cell death that contributes to normal development and tissue remodeling.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: A translocation moves a chromosome segment to a different location, often involving a nonhomologous chromosome, and can disrupt or rearrange genes/regulation.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: An inversion reverses the orientation of a chromosome segment.

canonical_catalog.source_reference: Teacher enrichment; Campbell Biology 13e Ch.15

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Engineered plasmids can be introduced into bacterial cells so inserted genes can be propagated and, when appropriate regulatory sequences are present, expressed.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Do not answer a generic “bond holding nucleotides together” prompt with hydrogen bonds. Phosphodiester bonds link adjacent nucleotides within a strand; hydrogen bonds stabilize complementary base pairing between strands/regions.

canonical_catalog.canonical_label: Typical DNA/RNA structure is not absolute
canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Treat double-stranded DNA and single-stranded RNA as typical cellular patterns, not universal rules across all nucleic acids and viruses.

canonical_catalog.canonical_label: Extra replication enzyme names are enrichment
canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: SSBPs, primase, DNA polymerase I/III, and detailed primer-removal machinery are scientifically useful teacher enrichment but are not current AP-required enzyme-name targets.
